answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
We support consequential accounting as the primary mechanism to quantify the system-level decarbonization —a metric not captured by current Scope 2 attributional accounting

Clarifying how consequential accounting can be used by companies for electricity projects in and outside of a company’s value chain: Companies that report energy attributes from a PPA or spot-market purchases in their contractual/market-based inventory should also be encouraged by GHG Protocol guidance to report the reduced emissions separately in the impact ledger using a consequential accounting methodology. We understand that GHG Protocol and other experts prefer use the concepts of induced emissions and avoided emissions when referring to project-based consequential accounting approaches. Winrock uses the term “reduced”, because in the jurisdictional / sectoral context, emissions aren’t avoided, rather measured as reduced at the system level from a conservative, jurisdiction specific baseline. There is not a need to specifically identify which emissions are avoided and induced, because emission reductions are measured at the full system level—in the context of electricity at the grid level.

To operationalize this the impact ledger for Scope 2 electricity could be split into two fields: One field for reduced emissions associated with EACs in the contractual/market-based inventory and another field for reduced emissions occurring outside of the contractual/market-based inventory boundaries. This would allow stakeholders to understand which consequential impacts are occurring inside and outside of the company’s value chain.

The consequential accounting subgroup’s proposal which was not released in this consultation provides a better basis as an approach than what the GHG Protocol has released.

While the subgroup’s proposal provides a good basis, clarity on what GHG Protocol recommends or permits as an additionality test is needed to make it complete. In addition, Winrock believes GHG P should recognize sectoral consequential accounting approaches for electricity projects too, such as the Standard for the Transformation of the Electric Power Sector (STEPS) in development by Environmental Resources Trust (ERT), a wholly owned non-profit subsidiary of Winrock.

The way that STEPS will work in concept for consequential accounting is as outlined in “Key Elements of a Sectoral Crediting Standard for the Energy Transition Accelerator ERT methodology”. ERT is finalizing STEPS for global consultation in 2026. The approach is different from project-based accounting in several ways. First, the sectoral standard’s participants will be national governments or authorized designees of the national government. Second, the standard is based on improvements in overall grid-level electric power sector emissions performance that surpass a Paris-aligned, performance standard. This performance threshold is adjusted to lower over time so that the crediting baseline stays conservative. This approach incentivizes long-term structural transformation of the sector by allowing for a range of intentional policy and regulatory shifts, operational investments and technical interventions to reduce emissions at the sector level rather than prescribing specific actions for crediting. Third, additionality in a sectoral approach is not established as it would be in many project-based approaches. The only “additionality test” that is relevant for STEPS is what GHG Protocol refers to in question 10 as a performance standard test. If a performance standard is set conservatively (below BAU), the additionality requirement is met. There are no regulatory or financial additionality tests for jurisdictional or sectoral crediting approaches. Lastly, because the crediting boundary of the system is the electricity grid in a given country (including captured plants, imports and exports of electricity from other countries), all emissions are captured, addressing concerns about leakage.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
The multiple-choice options are not well-suited to the range of potential scenarios for additionality, which could skew survey results for the GHG Protocol Secretariat. If “Not relevant/applicable” was an option, it would enable respondents to provide clearer responses. For example, if GHG Protocol is open to allowing different methodological approaches for consequential accounting, in some instances certain tests would not be applicable. It’s not a question of whether to require or make something optional, it’s a question of relevance. Below we provide clarity on whether something should be required, options, not required or is not relevant/applicable.

Regulatory test: Some demonstration of regulatory additionality should be required for all project-based methodologies. For sectoral standards this test is not applicable. In the setting of a performance standard, in most cases, regulatory additionality would be established because in meeting the performance standard, a country would need to enact new policies and regulations to achieve such an ambitious level of lower emissions that what would be projected in all estimates of what BAU would be in the future.

Timing test: This test (which is often called “prior consideration”) may be relevant for project-based approaches, but not in the case of performance standards or positive lists. However, individual project interventions are not reviewed or tested individually in a sectoral crediting approach, which considers overall emissions performance at the sector level, taking all contributing activities into consideration. Electricity projects that are financed and built without a REC offtaker are already financially viable and so would not pass the additionality test; therefore, any estimated avoided emissions should not be recorded in the impact ledger in a company’s inventory report.

Financial test: Optional for project-based approaches. Not applicable for sectoral or jurisdictional approaches. It would be helpful for corporate buyers to understand how much of a financial impact their intervention makes. But if a bank is willing to take the risk of financing it based on the corporate REC revenue, the financial analysis would not discredit the additionality aspect of the project. Also, asymmetric information on real internal rates of return can often allow project developers to look like they need the REC or energy transition carbon credit revenue, but they might not in reality.

Barrier test: Optional for project-based approaches. Not applicable for sectoral or jurisdictional approaches.

Common practice test: Optional for project-based approaches. Not applicable for sectoral or jurisdictional approaches.

Positive list: Optional for project-based approaches. Not applicable for sectoral approaches.

Performance standard test: As mentioned in response to question 18, the conservativeness of performance standard baseline is the additionality demonstration for the Environmental Resources Trust sectoral crediting approaches for the electricity sector and for jurisdictional crediting under TREES. For project-based approaches it may be relevant. (As an additional note, the characterization of a performance-based approach in the consultation materials [https://ghgprotocol.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/GHG-Protocol-Consequential-Electricity-Sector-Emissions-Impacts-Public-Consultation.pdf] on page 10 does not reflect how a performance standard is set under the future ERT methodology.) For a project-based methodology, this could be an optional test.

Contractual/tenor test: Optional for project-based approaches. Not applicable for sectoral or jurisdictional approaches.

First-of-its-kind test: Optional for project-based approaches. Not applicable for sectoral or jurisdictional approaches.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: We are highlighting what we believe is most feasible. Some of the other tests may be feasible, but we are not able to assess whether they will be replicably effective tests. As described in the answer in question 27, most test are not applicable to sectoral crediting methodologies.
